title: India Wants Its Diaspora Athletes Back. A 'Sports Passport' Could Make It Happen.
excerpt: The government has sent a proposal to the PMO that could let PIO and OCI athletes represent India without giving up their foreign passports — a first in Indian sports history.
body:
India does not allow dual citizenship. It never has. And for decades, that single legal fact has drained the country's talent pipeline in sports where it needs the most help — football, basketball, tennis, and athletics.

Now, for the first time, the government may be ready to bend.

The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has sent a proposal to the Prime Minister's Office and the Ministry of Home Affairs for a "Sports Passport" — a special eligibility pathway that would allow Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) to represent India in international competitions without requiring them to renounce their foreign citizenship.

## Why Now?

The timing is not accidental. India is preparing a bid for the 2036 Olympics, and the government knows that its medal tally in global multisport events remains embarrassingly thin relative to the country's population. In football, the disconnect is even more visible: the men's national team has been stuck outside the world's top 100 for years, even as players of Indian heritage represent other nations at the highest level.

At the 2026 FIFA World Cup — happening right now across the United States, Canada, and Mexico — at least four players of Indian origin are on the pitch. Sarpreet Singh plays for New Zealand. Samuel Moutoussamy represents DR Congo. Nishan Velupillay is in Australia's squad. Tahsin Jamshid suits up for Qatar. None of them plays for India.

## The Ryan Williams Precedent

The current system already has one high-profile convert. Ryan Williams, a midfielder born and raised in Australia, gave up his Australian passport in 2025 to represent India's football team. The process was neither simple nor fast, and it required a complete renunciation of his birth citizenship — a sacrifice that few professional athletes in established leagues are willing to make.

A Sports Passport would eliminate that barrier. Under the proposal, eligible athletes of Indian heritage could compete for India through a streamlined process, without giving up the passports that anchor their careers and residences abroad.

## Global Precedents

India would not be the first country to try this. Qatar built much of its national football team through fast-track citizenship for athletes of foreign origin, a strategy that helped it host and compete in the 2022 World Cup. Bahrain, Turkey, Spain, Hungary, and Austria have all used similar mechanisms to strengthen their national teams in sports where indigenous talent pools run thin.

The difference is that India's proposal focuses specifically on people who already have Indian heritage — PIO and OCI cardholders — rather than casting a wide net for any willing athlete. The framework is designed to reclaim a diaspora that numbers over 30 million people spread across more than 100 countries.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI families in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, the implications are personal. Indian-origin children who grow up playing competitive football, tennis, or athletics in Western systems currently have no pathway to represent India unless they abandon the citizenship of the country where they were raised. Many talented young athletes choose to compete for their country of birth — or simply walk away from international competition altogether.

A Sports Passport could change the calculus overnight. A young footballer in London with OCI status could, in theory, receive a call-up from the Indian national team without jeopardising her British passport. A tennis player in Melbourne with Indian parents could represent India at the Asian Games without renouncing Australian citizenship.

## The Timeline

Sources indicate the government could take six to eight months to evaluate the proposal before it is considered for approval. The proposal would likely require amendments to the Citizenship Act, and any changes would need to be coordinated between the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of External Affairs, and the relevant sports federations.

If approved, it could be one of the most significant developments in Indian sports history — not because it will produce instant medal winners, but because it would formally acknowledge what the diaspora has always known: Indian talent does not stop at India's borders.

## The Counterarguments

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Critics argue that a Sports Passport could undermine domestic development by importing ready-made talent rather than investing in grassroots infrastructure. Others worry about the integrity of national representation — whether athletes who grew up in different sporting cultures and systems can genuinely represent India's sporting identity.

These are legitimate concerns. But the current system, which loses athletes like Sarpreet Singh and Nishan Velupillay to other nations while India's football team languishes, is not working either. The Sports Passport proposal is a bet that opening the door is better than watching talent walk through someone else's.
